newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Red Cross says NKorea faces long-term flood blow.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross says NKorea faces long-term flood blow.

text.p: North Korea faces a long-term problem in feeding itself following autumn floods and heavy rains two years in succession, a senior Red Cross official in the country has reported.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said in its latest weekly bulletin it had just launched a new programme in the largely isolated communist country to feed 139,000 flood victims.

"A series of disasters have created food deficit problems and their impact may last for several years, given the losses of arable land," the bulletin quoted IFRC representative in Pyongyang OIle Gronning as saying.

According to the bulletin, the North Korean government had itself reported that this year's harvest would be two million tonnes short of target -- a shortfall of 40 per cent of the grain needed to feed the 26 million population through 1997.

Devastating floods following torrential rain in August and September of 1995 led the normally secretive state to open up to outside aid agencies, including the IFRC and the Rome-based World Food Programme.
Houses, roads, factories and grain stores in the west and north-west of the country were swept away and mines flooded, causing electricity shortages. Ricefields were covered with mud and rubble.

After months of relief efforts, during which there were widespread reports of near starvation in some areas and severe malnutrition in many regions, rains this year struck again, destroying bridges and irrigation works.

The IFRC, which links Red Cross and Red Crescent societies around the world including in North Korea, said its feeding programme for the worst affected people would continue until the October 1997 harvest.
It would also be distributing, through the country's own society, blankets and winter clothes to 28,000 families in 15 of the counties where the floods had hit hardest, the bulletin said.
Under the programme, the North Korean Red Cross would be distributing the equivalent of 450 grammes of rice or maize a day to the 139,000 target flood victims.

Some 550 baby goats would be provided to cooperative farms -- many of whose animal flocks were destroyed in the flooding -- to begin a livestock breeding programme in two mountainous counties, the IFRC said.
The programme is being funded through IFRC appeals for support to its member societies. The latest sought just over 13 million Swiss francs ($10,3 million).
